stimulus.text:
“'Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land,
Taught my benighted soul to understand
That there's a God, that there's a Saviour too:
Once I redemption neither sought nor knew.
Some view our sable race with scornful eye,
‘Their colour is a diabolic die.’
Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain,
May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train.”
— Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America,” in Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773)
stimulus.source_note: Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773). Public domain.

stem: Wheatley's direct address to “Christians” in the last four lines shows that her audience is

options.text: Enslaved Africans planning to rise against their owners
options.misconception: She addresses Christians, not enslaved rebels; nothing in the poem speaks to a planned uprising.

options.text: Members of the British Parliament debating the slave trade
options.misconception: Parliament never appears in the poem; she speaks to Christians in general, not to lawmakers.

options.text: White Christians, whom she challenges on their own religious terms
Native leaders deciding whether to side with the Patriots
options.misconception: Native leaders are not her audience; the poem's subject is Black people and white Christian readers.

rationales.C: “Remember, Christians” speaks straight to white readers, using their own faith — salvation open to all — against their scorn for Black people.
rationales.A: The poem calls on Christians to rethink their scorn; it does not call enslaved people to rise.
rationales.B: No Parliament appears here; her audience is the Christian reader, not a legislature.
rationales.D: Native peoples are absent from the poem; its argument runs between Black people and white Christians.
rationales.general:
1. Find who she names. “Remember, Christians” — she speaks to Christians, not to rebels or lawmakers.
2. Find her weapon. Their own faith: if salvation is open to all, Black people share in it.
3. Rule out the rest. No Parliament, no uprising, and no Native audience appears in the poem.
Remember: an author's audience is named in the address — read who is spoken to, not who you expect.
